**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Paper 2: Section A - Composition; Section B - Prescribed Texts; Section C - Creative Writing. Duration: two hours fifteen minutes.**

Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised answer will earn you little or no marks.

**SECTION A - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Say which picture is used (Picture B) and describe what it shows.
2. Link it to a personal story: the Saturday mornings at the stream.
3. Develop the scene: the work, the mother's saying, the laughter, the women's talk.
4. Show the change over time: university, the return to the stream.
5. Close with the meaning of the picture: dignity of work and joy in love.

**Model composition (515 words)**

I have chosen Picture B, which shows a woman crouching at the edge of a stream, wringing out a piece of cloth, while a small girl beside her laughs with all her heart. The picture reminded me of the Saturday mornings of my childhood, when my mother and I walked to the stream behind our village to wash the family's clothes.

Our village had no tap in those days. Every Saturday, before the sun grew fierce, Mama tied her wrapper tightly, balanced a basin of dirty clothes on her head and took my hand. I followed her down a narrow path through the bushes, carrying the bar of blue soap like a treasure. Birds sang in the trees, and the smell of wet earth followed us all the way. The water was cold and clear, and smooth rocks lay along the banks, as warm as sleeping animals when the sun reached them.

Mama worked quickly and with great skill. She soaked each garment, rubbed it with soap, beat it on a flat stone and wrung it until the water ran down her arms. Her back was bent and her hands were rough, but I never heard her complain. "Work is not a punishment, Lydia," she used to say. "It is what feeds us with pride." I was five and did not understand. I splashed my own small handkerchief in the shallow water, and when the cold spray flew into my face, I burst out laughing, exactly like the girl in the picture. My mother would smile at me over her shoulder, and for a moment all her tiredness disappeared.

Those mornings were not only about washing. The stream was where the women of the village met to talk. They exchanged news of births, quarrels and weddings, advised one another about sick children and sang old songs while they worked. Sometimes the youngest girls were allowed to carry the washed clothes home in small bundles, as proud as soldiers on parade. I listened, perched on a stone, and learnt more about courage and community than any classroom could have taught me.

Years later, when I left for university in the city, my life changed completely. I had taps, a washing machine and a laundry service, yet nothing seemed as clean or smelt as sweet as the clothes spread on the bushes beside our stream. During my first holiday I went back to the water with my mother, rolled up my sleeves and washed beside her as I had done as a child. She laughed at my clumsy hands and said I had forgotten everything. I laughed with her, and the water laughed too.

Now I am a nurse, and when the day's work is heavy, I think of that bent back and that stubborn smile. The picture seems to me to speak of more than hardship; it shows that where there is love, even the humblest duty can be turned into joy. That is the lesson my mother gave me beside the water, and I hope to pass it on to my own daughter one day.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A clear, visible connection with ONE picture (named in the first lines), a coherent story or description built on it, logical paragraphs, 500 to 550 words. |
| Expression | 8 | Descriptive and narrative language, sensory details, dialogue, a clear voice and an effective ending. |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct tenses, spelling and punctuation. |

**Common errors**

- Writing a composition with no real link to the picture (or mixing both pictures without a link): the connection must be explicit.
- Only describing the people in the picture, line by line, with no development: a good answer builds a story, a reflection or a vivid scene from it.
